prompt: Why is media production economically distinctive?
options: First-copy costs are high; reproduction marginal costs are near zero (non-rival information goods)
correctAnswer: First-copy costs are high; reproduction marginal costs are near zero (non-rival information goods)
explanation: Media businesses have a peculiar cost structure: a New York Times investigation may take months and tens of thousands of dollars to produce, but reproducing it for one additional reader costs essentially zero. Combined with partial excludability and experience-good characteristics, this produces market structures that rarely settle into textbook competitive equilibrium and that tend toward winner-takes-most distributions.

prompt: What did Jean Tirole and Jean-Charles Rochet's work on two-sided markets describe?
options: Markets where prices on each side interact through network effects between them
correctAnswer: Markets where prices on each side interact through network effects between them
explanation: Tirole's two-sided-market theory (recognised by the 2014 Nobel) showed that pricing on each side of platforms-with-cross-network-effects is not set independently. Media's classic two-sided market — content for audiences, audiences for advertisers — is the canonical case: cross-subsidies are common, and the market structure does not behave like a standard one-sided market.

prompt: Roughly how many US newspapers closed between 2005 and 2024?
explanation: Around 2,500 US newspapers closed between 2005 and 2024, with total newsroom employment falling by more than half. The 'news desert' phenomenon — counties with no local news organisation at all — affected over 200 US counties by the mid-2020s. The contraction was driven by the collapse of classified advertising and the diversion of display advertising to digital platforms.

prompt: Which book applied the 'attention economy' frame to digital media in 2016?
options: The Attention Merchants by Tim Wu
correctAnswer: The Attention Merchants by Tim Wu
explanation: Tim Wu's The Attention Merchants (2016) traces the development of attention-capture industries from 19th-century newspaper hawkers through broadcast advertising to digital platforms. The framing — building on Herbert Simon's earlier observation that information abundance produces attention scarcity — has become standard in contemporary media-economics discussion.

prompt: Match each economic concept to its application to media:

pairs.right: One person's consumption does not diminish another's; reproduction cost near zero
Quality cannot be assessed before consumption
Content for audiences subsidised by advertising paid by another side

explanation: These three concepts together explain much of why media markets behave differently from textbook competitive markets. The non-rival nature drives high-fixed-cost / low-marginal-cost dynamics; the experience-good property complicates pricing and quality competition; the two-sided structure produces the cross-subsidies and bundling patterns that characterise advertising-funded media.

prompt: What does CPM stand for in advertising?
explanation: CPM (cost per thousand, from the Roman numeral M for thousand) measures the cost of reaching a thousand audience-member exposures with an ad. It was the standard pricing metric across mid-20th-century display advertising, allowing comparison across very different media properties.

prompt: By the 1980s, classified advertising provided what share of typical metropolitan US daily newspaper revenue?
explanation: By the 1980s, classified advertising provided 30–40% of total revenue for typical metropolitan US dailies and a higher share for local and community papers. The classifieds business depended on the newspaper's local-information monopoly — there was nowhere else to advertise a used car or post a help-wanted listing locally.

prompt: The site that systematically broke newspaper classified-advertising monopolies in the 2000s was _________.
explanation: Craigslist, founded 1995 by Craig Newmark and expanded nationally through the early 2000s, handled used cars, apartments, jobs, and personals at zero or low cost. Combined with vertical-search sites (Monster, Indeed, Zillow), Craigslist drove an estimated 75% collapse in US newspaper classified revenue from peak.

prompt: When did the US TV ad market peak before its post-2018 decline?
explanation: The combined US TV ad market peaked around 2018 at about $73 billion and has been falling progressively since. Cord-cutting, the digital-platform shift, and the relative measurement and targeting advantages of digital platforms drove the decline. Broadcast networks have responded with addressable-television initiatives, ad-supported streaming tiers, and digital extensions.

prompt: Match each broadcast-advertising term to its meaning:

pairs.right: Annual May–June sales process where networks sell next season's inventory in advance
Sales filling remaining inventory closer to airdate, often at higher CPMs
Compensation to advertiser for ratings shortfall vs. guaranteed delivery

explanation: The upfronts, scatter market, and make-good system together institutionalised the broadcast-era sales process. The whole apparatus assumed a small number of large network properties commanding most of the available audience attention; its structure has been largely inherited by the streaming-platform ad-supported sales operations of the 2020s.

prompt: When did the New York Times launch its metered paywall?
explanation: The New York Times launched its metered paywall in March 2011. Allowing a small number of free articles per month before requiring subscription preserved most search-and-social-referred traffic while monetising the heaviest readers. By 2024 the Times had over 11 million digital subscribers — a transformative success that reshaped the industry's revenue mix.

prompt: Which kind of journalism has the subscription model worked best for?
options: National brands with distinctive value propositions (NYT, WSJ, FT, Economist)
correctAnswer: National brands with distinctive value propositions (NYT, WSJ, FT, Economist)
explanation: National brands with distinctive value propositions have built large digital subscriber bases. Local papers without comparable distinctive content, and tabloid-format papers competing on entertainment value, have found subscriptions much harder. The result is a hollowed-out local-news layer where the subscription model has not produced sustainable economics.

prompt: The platform that combines email newsletters with subscription payment infrastructure for individual writers is _________.
explanation: Substack (2017) produced a successful new layer of independent journalism. Writers including Bari Weiss, Andrew Sullivan, Glenn Greenwald, Matt Taibbi, Heather Cox Richardson, and Casey Newton built six-figure subscription businesses; total Substack writer payouts crossed $300 million by 2024.

prompt: The Guardian's digital revenue model is distinctive because it:
options: Combines a voluntary-membership model with no general paywall, plus event tickets and other revenue
Relies entirely on the British government
correctAnswer: Combines a voluntary-membership model with no general paywall, plus event tickets and other revenue
explanation: The Guardian operates a voluntary-membership model that asks readers to support the publication without imposing a paywall on most content. Combined with event ticket sales, philanthropic gifts, and limited advertising, the model has produced sustainable economics with strong reader identification — though the approach is harder to replicate at smaller publications.

prompt: Match each direct-funding model to its description:

pairs.right: Free articles up to a monthly limit, then subscription required
Direct subscriber payments to individual creators
Voluntary support without paywall; relationship-not-transaction framing

explanation: These three direct-funding models have different operational characteristics. Metered paywalls preserve traffic while monetising heavy readers; patronage scales the subscription model down to individuals; membership de-emphasises the transactional relationship in favour of sustained support. Each has a different fit to different content categories and audience relationships.

prompt: What was the 1948 Paramount antitrust decree?
options: A government takeover of Hollywood studios
Forced divestiture of theatre chains by the major Hollywood studios
An export tax on Hollywood films
correctAnswer: Forced divestiture of theatre chains by the major Hollywood studios
explanation: The 1948 Paramount antitrust decree forced the vertically-integrated Hollywood studios (MGM, Paramount, Warner, RKO, 20th Century Fox) to divest their theatre chains. The decree ended the studio system's vertical integration of production, distribution, and exhibition; the cable era saw partial reintegration through different combinations.

prompt: What did Disney acquire in 2019 for approximately $71 billion?
explanation: Disney's 2019 acquisition of 21st Century Fox's entertainment assets brought 20th Century Fox studios, FX, the Star network, and major sports rights (with the regional sports networks subsequently divested). The deal made Disney the largest single content owner in Hollywood and significantly accelerated the streaming-wars consolidation.

prompt: The German conglomerate that owns Penguin Random House, RTL Group, and Gruner + Jahr is _________.
explanation: Bertelsmann is the dominant European media conglomerate, owning the world's largest English-language book publisher (Penguin Random House), one of Europe's largest broadcasters (RTL Group), and major magazine and music interests. The company has been continuously controlled by the Mohn family through a foundation structure since the 1970s.

prompt: Gentzkow and Shapiro's empirical work on US newspaper slant found that:
options: Newspapers' slant is determined entirely by ownership
Ownership matters less than reader-preference market-pull effects
All US newspapers have identical coverage
Owners cannot influence coverage at all
correctAnswer: Ownership matters less than reader-preference market-pull effects
explanation: Gentzkow and Shapiro's empirical analyses find that newspapers tend to align with reader preferences in their markets, and ownership effects are detectable but smaller than market-pull effects. The finding moderates the most polemical accounts of how concentration affects coverage, while acknowledging that ownership effects are real and that contemporary platform-power concerns may behave differently.

prompt: Match each major media conglomerate to a flagship property:

pairs.right: ESPN, ABC, Pixar, Marvel, Disney+, theme parks
NBC networks, Universal Pictures, Peacock, broadband infrastructure
WSJ, NY Post, Times newspapers, Fox News, Fox Sports

explanation: These three holdings illustrate different consolidation patterns: Disney's content-and-experience integration; Comcast's distribution-plus-content vertical model; the Murdoch holdings' news-and-broadcast cross-portfolio. Together with Warner Bros. Discovery, Sony, Paramount Global, and the streaming-tech giants, they account for most of the global content-production layer.

prompt: How is the BBC primarily funded?
explanation: The BBC is funded primarily by the household licence fee (£3.7 billion in 2024), which is paid by anyone watching live broadcast television or BBC iPlayer. The model preserves independence from advertiser pressure but is politically vulnerable as smaller cohorts of younger viewers consume primarily streaming content and resist paying for traditional broadcast.

prompt: ProPublica was founded in 2008 with seed funding from:
explanation: ProPublica was founded in 2008 with seed funding from the Sandler Foundation. Its model — non-profit investigative journalism funded by foundation grants and individual donations, with content distributed in partnership with traditional publishers — has become an influential template for the broader US non-profit news sector.

prompt: Jeff Bezos acquired the Washington Post in 2013 for approximately $_____ million.
explanation: Bezos's 2013 acquisition of the Washington Post for $250 million was followed by a decade of growth in digital subscriptions, investment in newsroom expansion, and a return to profitability — until 2024–2025, when the publication faced renewed political and editorial pressure that has tested the billionaire-owner model.

prompt: Which Qatari-funded broadcaster operates with substantial editorial independence within constraints set by Qatari regional-policy interests?
explanation: Al Jazeera (founded 1996) is Qatari-funded and operates with substantial but not unlimited editorial independence. The line between PSB-style independence and state-controlled-media is contested; Al Jazeera sits in the middle ground. RT, CGTN, and Press TV are more clearly state-controlled media in the strict sense.

prompt: Match each press-funding mechanism to a country or example:

pairs.right: Nordic countries — long-established support for newspapers below certain market positions
Canada — government-funded reporters placed in underserved communities
US — MacArthur, Knight, Ford, Open Society funding non-profit news

explanation: Different countries have built different mixes of public, foundation, and private funding for journalism. Nordic press subsidies have not produced obvious editorial dependence; the Canadian Local Journalism Initiative addresses local-news deserts; the US foundation ecosystem is one of the most developed but still small relative to lost commercial revenue.

prompt: Roughly what share of global digital ad revenue do Google and Meta together command?
explanation: Google (Alphabet) and Meta together account for roughly 60% of global digital ad revenue. The combined revenue of these two companies' advertising businesses exceeded $400 billion in 2024 — more than the entire global newspaper industry's peak revenue at any point in history.

prompt: The Australian News Media Bargaining Code (2021):
options: Required platforms to negotiate with news publishers over content compensation
correctAnswer: Required platforms to negotiate with news publishers over content compensation
explanation: The Australian Code was the first major regulatory intervention requiring platforms to negotiate with news publishers over content compensation. After Meta briefly blocked news content from Australian Facebook, both Google and Meta reached commercial agreements with major publishers. The model has been imitated and modified in Canada, France, Germany, and elsewhere.

prompt: Approximately what was Amazon's 2024 advertising revenue, in billions of dollars?
explanation: Amazon's advertising business has grown rapidly into a third major platform-side player alongside Google and Meta. The combination of search advertising on Amazon.com, Amazon Prime Video advertising (rolled out 2024), Twitch advertising, and the broader DSP gave Amazon over $50 billion in 2024 ad revenue.

prompt: Why are the 2023 US DOJ and EU antitrust cases against Google's ad-tech business significant?
options: They sought to break up search
They specifically targeted the ad-tech intermediation margins between advertisers and publishers
They have already produced full divestiture
correctAnswer: They specifically targeted the ad-tech intermediation margins between advertisers and publishers
explanation: Google's Ad Tech stack (DoubleClick, AdSense, AdMob, AdX) intermediates much of the digital ad market, taking margins at multiple layers between advertisers and publishers. The 2023 DOJ and EU cases specifically target these intermediation margins. Whether structural remedies emerge from these cases is one of the central open questions of late-decade competition policy.

prompt: Match each platform-era policy to its description:

pairs.right: Imposes rules on designated 'gatekeeper' platforms regarding self-preferencing and interoperability
Requires platforms to negotiate with news publishers over content compensation
Google feature summarising search results with AI-generated text, threatening publisher referral traffic

explanation: These three illustrate the regulatory and product-side dynamics shaping the platform–publisher relationship. The DMA and bargaining codes attempt to constrain platform power; AI Overviews illustrate how product-side platform changes can substantially shift the underlying economics regardless of regulatory intervention. The combined effect on publisher economics is one of the central uncertainties of the late 2020s.
